## Statement

MAIC-style weighting is defined for one pairwise comparison against one aggregate study, so a two-stage weighting workflow that outputs separately adjusted contrasts with only marginal standard errors loses the covariance induced by a shared common arm and the covariance induced by shared weight estimation. Regression-based population adjustment already solves this at the network level: multilevel network meta-regression is a one-stage arm-level likelihood valid for networks of any size (Phillippo et al. 2020, doi:10.1111/rssa.12579), implemented in multinma since 2020, where multi-arm studies carry correlated multivariate-normal random effects (Perren et al. 2025, doi:10.1177/0272989X251389887). What is open is the weighting branch: there is no arm-level MAIC-style estimator, and no sandwich or multivariate bootstrap variance estimator for weighted multi-arm contrasts that also carries weight-estimation uncertainty has been derived or benchmarked. The same split holds in cpaic, an unreleased development package on GitHub that is not on CRAN: at commit 9d150e9 cmlnmr() gives within-study deviations from a study baseline the standard 0.5 NMA correlation, while cmaic() and cstc() refuse IPD studies with more than two arms rather than processing them pairwise. The same covariance is lost without any multi-arm trial present. Where a sparse network admits single-arm studies by matching each to a comparator arm of an existing randomized trial, several pseudo-contrasts can be built from the same comparator arm, so their errors are correlated through shared control observations exactly as contrasts are correlated within a multi-arm trial; published implementations nonetheless enter them into the network likelihood as independent evidence, and in a late-onset Pompe disease network admitting the matched single-arm studies reversed the direction of the headline comparison.

## Why it is open

Multi-arm trials produce correlated contrasts because they share a common arm, and a network likelihood needs that correlation; a two-stage pipeline that adjusts one contrast at a time and passes on only marginal standard errors has nowhere to store it. Weight estimation adds a second source of correlation between contrasts that naive variance formulas ignore. Neither is a theoretical obstacle, because one weight set can feed a joint arm-level outcome model and a multivariate bootstrap that re-estimates the weights recovers the full contrast covariance; the obstacle is that nobody has derived, implemented or benchmarked this for the weighting branch. The consequence surfaces as distorted precision and as spurious or masked inconsistency rather than as an obvious failure, which is why nobody is forced to confront it.

## What has been tried

::: {.table-scroll}

| Work | What it contributes |
|---|---|
| [Phillippo et al., 2020, Multilevel network meta-regression for population-adjusted treatment comparisons, JRSS-A](https://doi.org/10.1111/rssa.12579) | Defines an individual-level regression model and fits aggregate data by integrating over the covariate distribution to form the likelihood; this is the arm-based one-stage population-adjusted estimator the source says does not exist, and it is valid for networks of any size including multi-arm trials. |
| [multinma: Bayesian Network Meta-Analysis of Individual and Aggregate Data (version 0.9.1)](https://cran.r-project.org/package=multinma) | Working implementation: nma() fits ML-NMR with arm-based likelihoods, and multi-arm studies receive correlated multivariate-normal random effects. |
| [Perren, Pedder, Welton and Phillippo, 2026, Network Meta-Analysis with Class Effects: A Practical Guide and Model Selection Algorithm](https://doi.org/10.1177/0272989X251389887) | States the multi-arm covariance parameterization used in multinma, confirming that studies with more than one non-baseline arm have multiple correlated random effects modeled as multivariate normal. |
| [Phillippo et al., 2019, Population adjustment methods for indirect comparisons: a review of NICE technology appraisals](https://doi.org/10.1017/S0266462319000333) | Cited by the audit as counter-evidence that the problem is real in practice: larger treatment networks were commonplace in NICE appraisals (10 of 18) while the population adjustment methods in use could not account for them. |
| [cpaic, unreleased development package on GitHub (not on CRAN), commit 9d150e9](https://github.com/choxos/cpaic) | cmlnmr() jointly fits IPD and aggregate arms by integrating the individual-level model over each aggregate study's covariate distribution, and cmlnmr_random.R gives multi-arm deviations from a study baseline the standard 0.5 NMA correlation; cmaic() and cstc() support two-arm IPD studies only. |
| [Shohet et al. 2024, Journal of Comparative Effectiveness Research](https://doi.org/10.57264/cer-2024-0045) | Builds a rare-disease network by pairing each single-arm study with the comparator arm of an existing randomized trial chosen to minimize a distance over aggregate baseline characteristics, then enters the resulting pseudo-contrasts as independent evidence in the network likelihood while recording the reuse of comparator-arm evidence as a limitation; admitting the matched single-arm studies reverses the direction of the headline comparison. |
| [Goring et al. 2016, Research Synthesis Methods](https://doi.org/10.1002/jrsm.1204) | Sets out the analytic options for treatment networks having no common comparator, the sparse-network setting in which single-arm studies are matched to existing comparator arms rather than left out. |

:::

## Probable solution or research direction

Do not rebuild the one-stage arm-level likelihood, which ML-NMR in multinma already provides; extend the weighting branch to match it. Derive a MAIC-style estimator that applies one weight set to a joint arm-level model, with a sandwich or multivariate bootstrap variance that accounts for weight estimation as well as the outcome model, and give two-stage implementations a joint covariance matrix to export instead of marginal standard errors. Benchmark it in simulations that inject three-arm and four-arm studies with correlated contrasts and unequal variances, reporting variance recovery, inconsistency inflation and undercoverage, with ML-NMR as the reference rather than as the thing being replaced. In cpaic the concrete step is multi-arm support for cmaic() and cstc(), which currently reject such studies outright.

## Verification

::: {.verification-trail}
**Verdict.** Overstated. 2 independent auditors judged the claim as stated too strong. MAIC-style weighting is defined for a single pairwise comparison against one aggregate study, so weighting-based PAIC applied contrast by contrast loses the covariance induced by a shared common arm. Regression-based population adjustment already solves this: multilevel network meta-regression (Phillippo et al. 2020, implemented in multinma) is a one-stage arm-level likelihood that keeps multi-arm structure intact. The open part is a weighting-based arm-level estimator and a variance estimator for it that accounts for weight estimation.

**The source said.** "MAIC-style weighting is defined for one pairwise comparison against one aggregate study, so a multi-arm trial is processed contrast by contrast and the covariance induced by the shared common arm is never carried into the network likelihood. Standard NMA software handles that structure correctly, but it sits downstream of the weighting step and is not wired into it."

**What was wrong with it.** The source claimed no arm-based or multivariate PAIC estimator preserving multi-arm covariance is available, and cited nothing; the literature auditor found that multilevel network meta-regression is exactly that estimator and has been on CRAN in multinma since 2020 (doi:10.1111/rssa.12579), and the code auditor found cpaic's cmlnmr() already implements the shared-baseline multi-arm correlation. The code auditor also rejected the framing that it is not established whether weighting before contrast formation preserves the correct covariance: weighting is not inherently pairwise, and the weighted covariance is estimable by joint estimating equations or a bootstrap that re-estimates the weights, so this is undone work rather than an unverifiable assumption.

**Revised by the full-text reading.** Applied full-text reading.

merged-in
:   **absorbed a proposal the reading raised separately: Single-arm matching into networks leaves induced dependence unmodelled** 2 citation(s) added. The drafter disagreed with placing it here: The covariance half of this proposal merges cleanly: reusing one comparator arm across several matched pseudo-contrasts induces the same shared-data correlation that a two-stage pipeline exporting only marginal standard errors cannot carry, and the fix is the same joint covariance HET-02 already asks for. The second half does not merge as neatly. Residual bias from imperfect matching between a single arm and its chosen comparator is an unanchored-comparison problem with no randomized anchor, closer to the external-control and overlap entries than to multi-arm covariance, and HET-02 as written proposes no diagnostic for matching adequacy. If HET-02 takes on matched single-arm pseudo-contrasts, its research direction should either name a matching-adequacy diagnostic or hand that half to an unanchored-comparison entry rather than let it fall between the two.

Citation corrected
:   **normalized a citation year: 'Perren, Pedder, Welton and Phillippo, 2025, Network Meta-Analysis with Class Effects: A Practical Guide and Model Selection Algorithm' -> 'Perren, Pedder, Welton and Phillippo, 2026, Network Meta-Analysis with Class Effects: A Practical Guide and Model Selection Algorithm'** 10.1177/0272989X251389887 is cited with two different years across the registry. CrossRef gives 2025 online and 2026 in print; the issue year is used throughout.

closure-upheld
:   **6 findings from the reading assert this problem is open; the closure was re-examined and stands** Put to an independent reviewer with the closing auditors' reasoning, the work they relied on, and the new findings in view together. None of the findings contradicts the closure's cited one-stage ML-NMR result or show that its multi-arm likelihood fails to retain shared-arm covariance. The 2019 review and the gastric-cancer example document exactly the residual already conceded: applied pairwise workflows can treat dependent adjusted inputs as independent. The other findings concern standard NMA implementation, contribution matrices, or analogous non-PAIC settings, not an arm-level MAIC estimator or a joint weighted variance procedure. They therefore support the retained narrow problem in the weighting branch rather than reopen the stronger claim. (reviewer confidence: high)

Flagged for reopening
:   **10 findings from the reading assert this problem is open while the registry carries `overstated`** Flagged, not applied: reversing an earlier audit's closure needs the closure's own evidence re-examined alongside this, which the reading did not do. See documentation/audit/reading/PROPOSED.md.

Literature and prior-art check
:   **partially-solved / overstated.** The claim 'No arm-based or multivariate PAIC estimator that preserves multi-arm covariance is currently available' is contradicted by work the entry does not cite. Phillippo et al. (2020) multilevel network meta-regression is exactly a one-stage individual-level (arm-based) likelihood for population adjustment: 'An individual level regression model is defined, and aggregate data are fitted by integrating over the covariate distribution to form the likelihood', and it applies to 'networks of any size'. It is implemented in multinma 0.9.1. Perren, Pedder, Welton & Phillippo (2025) describe the same package's multi-arm handling verbatim: 'Studies with more than 1 nontreatment arm therefore have multiple RE, which are correlated and modeled using a multivariate normal distribution.' So the arm-based, multi-arm-preserving population-adjusted estimator exists and has been in CRAN software since 2020. What remains open is narrower and real: MAIC-style weighting itself has no arm-based extension, and no sandwich or multivariate bootstrap variance estimator for weighted multi-arm contrasts that also carries weight-estimation uncertainty has been derived or benchmarked. The 'Standard NMA software handles multi-arm correlated contrasts maturely' claim is correct.
    Cites doi:10.1111/rssa.12579: Provides the arm-based one-stage likelihood for population adjustment that the entry says does not exist, valid for networks of any size including multi-arm trials..
    Cites cran:multinma 0.9.1: Working implementation: nma() fits ML-NMR with arm-based likelihoods; multi-arm studies get correlated multivariate-normal random effects..
    Cites doi:10.1177/0272989X251389887: States the multi-arm covariance parameterization used in multinma, confirming multi-arm correlation is carried in the likelihood..

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens
:   **partially-solved / overstated.** C2, C5, C7, and C8 are technically sound with appropriate implementation. Weighting is not inherently pairwise: one set of patient weights can feed a joint arm-level outcome model, and joint estimating equations or a multivariate bootstrap that re-estimates the weights can recover the full contrast covariance. Thus C4 is framed incorrectly; the weighted covariance need not equal the unweighted covariance, but it is estimable rather than an intrinsically unverified assumption. At cpaic commit 9d150e9, cmaic() and cstc() reject IPD studies with more than two arms rather than processing them pairwise. More importantly, cmlnmr() is already a population-adjusted, joint arm-level estimator and implements the standard shared-baseline multi-arm random-effects correlation. This directly refutes C6 and the statement that covariance is never carried. The remaining open part is multi-arm support for the two-stage cMAIC and cSTC paths, including export of their joint covariance. C3's claim about what workflows often do is unsourced.
    Cites choxos/cpaic@9d150e9cad88f2e6fbcd94dbb92c3dee3b7c2dca: Implements a one-stage model that jointly fits IPD and aggregate arms while integrating over aggregate-study covariate distributions..
    Cites choxos/cpaic@9d150e9cad88f2e6fbcd94dbb92c3dee3b7c2dca: Preserves the standard covariance among random-effects contrasts sharing a baseline arm in cMLNMR..

Decision path
:   `R3:partially-solved(n=2) → R8:overstated-majority(n=2)`

:::

## How the evidence falls in time

10 papers in the reviewed corpus bear on this problem, published 2012 to 2019. Partial progress is on the record, and later work still calls this open. Both belong in view.

It is also being **closed in pieces**: partial results come from more than one paper in more than one year, each covering a different part.

::: {.table-scroll}

| Year | Says | Paper |
|---|---|---|
| 2012 | partly addresses it | Consistency and inconsistency in network meta-analysis: model estimation using multivariate meta-regression |
| 2013 | partly addresses it | Evidence synthesis for decision making 6: embedding evidence synthesis in probabilistic cost-effectiveness analysis |
| 2013 | partly addresses it | Evidence synthesis for decision making 7: a reviewer's checklist |
| 2013 | confirms it is open | Methods used to conduct and report Bayesian mixed treatment comparisons published in the medical literature: a systematic review |
| 2015 | confirms it is open | 'Arm-based' parameterization for network meta-analysis |
| 2017 | confirms it is open | Second-line Treatments for Advanced Gastric Cancer: A Network Meta-Analysis of Overall Survival Using Parametric Modelling Methods |
| 2018 | partly addresses it | Assessing the consistency assumptions underlying network meta-regression using aggregate data |
| 2018 | confirms it is open | Estimating the contribution of studies in network meta-analysis: paths, flows and streams |
| 2018 | confirms it is open | Large-scale external validation and comparison of prognostic models: an application to chronic obstructive pulmonary disease |
| 2019 | confirms it is open | Population Adjustment Methods for Indirect Comparisons: A Review of National Institute for Health and Care Excellence Technology Appraisals |
